card.title: Mass and inertia
card.body: **Inertia** is an object's natural tendency to resist any change in its velocity — staying at rest if at rest, or keeping constant velocity if already moving. **Mass** ($m$) is the scalar quantity that measures how much inertia an object has; it stays the same everywhere and is distinct from weight ($W = mg$).
card.says: more mass means more stubbornness against starting, stopping, or turning.
card.from: Galileo's thought experiments and Newton's framing of motion: inertia is a property of matter itself, not a force.
card.useWhen: comparing how hard it is to accelerate different objects, or separating constant **mass** ($\text{kg}$) from gravity-dependent **weight** ($\text{N}$).
card.example: An astronaut of mass $m = 60\text{ kg}$ weighs $W = 60 \times 9.8 = 588\text{ N}$ on Earth ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$) and $W = 60 \times 1.6 = 96\text{ N}$ on the Moon ($g_{\text{Moon}} = 1.6\text{ m/s}^2$), yet their mass — and inertia — remains $60\text{ kg}$ in both places.
card.analogy: Pushing an empty shopping cart is easy, while pushing a cart loaded with water bottles takes far more effort to start, stop, or steer around a corner.
